levels.title: Film & TV in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how still frames became movies and then television, and name the crafts that go into every film.

levels.title: The Illusion of Motion
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a quick run of still pictures tricks the eye and brain into seeing smooth movement.

levels.title: Frames per Second
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a frame rate is and why sound films settled on 24 frames every second.

levels.title: Muybridge's Galloping Horse
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Eadweard Muybridge's row of cameras settled whether a galloping horse ever lifts all four hooves.

levels.title: Edison's Peep Show
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Kinetoscope, the one-viewer movie cabinet built in Edison's lab, and why projection overtook it.

levels.title: The Lumières' First Screening
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Lumière brothers' 1895 Paris show, films projected for a paying crowd, counts as cinema's birth.

levels.title: Méliès and the Trick Film
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Georges Méliès used stop tricks and staged scenes to make films of fantasy, like A Trip to the Moon.

levels.title: The Great Train Robbery
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how The Great Train Robbery of 1903 told a story by cutting between places.

levels.title: How a Projector Works
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a projector's claw and shutter hold each frame still, then hide it while the film moves, so the picture never smears.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Moving Pictures
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how inventors turned photographs into projected moving pictures that could tell a story.

levels.title: The Nickelodeon Boom
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how five-cent storefront theaters made movies a cheap, everyday entertainment.

levels.title: Why Hollywood?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why American filmmaking moved from the East Coast to Southern California in the 1910s.

levels.title: Alice Guy-Blaché
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the career of Alice Guy-Blaché, one of the first directors to film made-up stories.

levels.title: Griffith and The Birth of a Nation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how D. W. Griffith's film techniques shaped the feature film and why his most famous film is condemned for its racism.

levels.title: Silent Comedy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton built comedy out of timing, stunts and pure movement.

levels.title: A Night at the Silent Movies
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how silent films were shown, with intertitles, live music and grand movie palaces.

levels.title: German Expressionism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how films like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari used twisted sets and deep shadows to show inner terror.

levels.title: Soviet Montage
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Sergei Eisenstein cut shots against each other to stir an audience, as in Battleship Potemkin.

levels.title: Nanook and the First Documentaries
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Nanook of the North set out to show and why some of its scenes were staged.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Silent Screen
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how silent films grew into a full art of image, gesture and music before sound arrived.

levels.title: From Script to Screen
levels.objective: After this level you can name the five stages of making a film, from development to distribution, and what happens in each.

levels.title: The Screenplay
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a screenplay is laid out and why one page is reckoned at about one minute of screen time.

levels.title: Storyboards and Shot Lists
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how storyboards and shot lists plan a scene before a camera rolls.

levels.title: Who Does What on a Film Set
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the jobs of the director, producer, cinematographer, gaffer, grip and script supervisor.

levels.title: Shot Sizes
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a wide shot, a medium shot and a close-up apart and say what each one is good for.

levels.title: Camera Angles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how high, low and tilted camera angles change how powerful or uneasy a character seems.

levels.title: Moving the Camera
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how pans, tilts, dolly shots, crane shots and handheld shots move a viewer through a scene.

levels.title: Lenses and Focus
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a lens's focal length and depth of field decide what looks near, far, sharp or soft.

levels.title: Lighting a Scene
levels.objective: After this level you can explain three-point lighting and how high-key and low-key lighting set a mood.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Shooting a Scene
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how planning, crew, camera and light work together to capture a single scene.

levels.title: What Editing Does
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how an editor chooses, orders and trims shots, from cutting film by hand to editing software.

levels.title: Invisible Editing
levels.objective: After this level you can explain continuity editing and the match on action, which hide cuts so a scene feels unbroken.

levels.title: The 180-Degree Rule
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the 180-degree rule keeps characters on the same sides of the screen so viewers stay oriented.

levels.title: Shot, Reverse Shot
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how shot, reverse shot and eyeline matches build a conversation out of separate shots.

levels.title: Cross-Cutting
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how cutting between two lines of action happening at once builds suspense.

levels.title: Jump Cuts and Match Cuts
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a jump cut from a match cut and explain the effect each has on a viewer.

levels.title: The Kuleshov Effect
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Kuleshov experiment showed that viewers read an actor's face from the shots around it.

levels.title: Sound in the Story, Sound for Us
levels.objective: After this level you can tell diegetic sound, which the characters can hear, from non-diegetic sound, which only the audience hears.

levels.title: Foley and Sound Design
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Foley artists and sound designers create footsteps, punches and whole worlds of sound after filming.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Cutting and Sound
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how editing and sound turn a pile of shots into a scene that feels continuous.

levels.title: The Talkies Arrive
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why The Jazz Singer's synchronized sound in 1927 upended Hollywood so quickly, and what it cost silent stars and cameras.

levels.title: The Big Studios
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the major studios owned the whole chain, from making films to the theaters that showed them.

levels.title: The Star System
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why studios signed actors to long contracts and carefully built their public images.

levels.title: The Production Code
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Hollywood censored itself under the Production Code from 1934 and why a ratings system replaced it in 1968.

levels.title: Technicolor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how three-strip Technicolor recorded color and why black and white stayed common into the 1960s.

levels.title: Citizen Kane
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Citizen Kane's deep focus, low angles and jumbled timeline made it a film that filmmakers study.

levels.title: The Hollywood Blacklist
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Hollywood blacklist began in 1947, how blacklisted writers kept working in secret, and how it ended.

levels.title: The Paramount Decision
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Supreme Court's 1948 Paramount ruling forced studios to sell their theaters and weakened the studio system.

levels.title: Widescreen Fights Back
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why movies went wider and bigger in the 1950s as television kept audiences at home.

levels.title: Milestone: How Hollywood Made Movies
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the invention of film, the craft of shooting and cutting, and the studio system into one picture of how a classic Hollywood film was made.

levels.title: What a Genre Promises
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a genre works as a promise between filmmakers and audiences about what they will feel.

levels.title: The Western
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Western became America's defining genre and how its picture of Native Americans changed over time.

levels.title: The Musical
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how musicals use song and dance to show feelings too big for speech.

levels.title: Screwball Comedy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why fast-talking screwball comedies of the 1930s pitted sharp-witted couples against each other.

levels.title: Horror
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why audiences choose to be scared and how horror films build dread before the shock.

levels.title: Film Noir
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why film noir's shadowy crime stories flourished in the 1940s and what gave them their dark look.

levels.title: Science Fiction
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why science fiction films use imagined futures and visitors to talk about fears of their own time.

levels.title: Suspense and Surprise
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Alfred Hitchcock's difference between surprise and suspense, and why giving the audience information builds tension.

levels.title: When Genres Bend
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how parodies and revisionist films bend a genre's rules, and why that only works once the rules are familiar.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Genres and Why They Work
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why genres work and how filmmakers keep familiar formulas fresh.

levels.title: Italian Neorealism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why postwar Italian filmmakers shot real streets with nonprofessional actors, as in Bicycle Thieves.

levels.title: The French New Wave
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how young French critics turned directors in the late 1950s broke Hollywood's rules with cheap, loose filmmaking.

levels.title: Kurosawa and Rashomon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rashomon told one event from clashing points of view and why its 1951 prize opened the West to Japanese film.

levels.title: Ozu's Quiet Style
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Yasujirō Ozu's low, still camera and simple cuts turned family life into drama.

levels.title: Satyajit Ray
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali brought a realist style to Indian cinema.

levels.title: Songs in Indian Popular Cinema
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why popular Hindi films weave song and dance into their stories and use playback singers.

levels.title: Hong Kong Action
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Hong Kong studios turned martial arts and stunt choreography into a style copied around the world.

levels.title: Nollywood
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Nigeria's film industry grew from cheap video films sold on cassettes in the 1990s.

levels.title: Film Festivals
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what festivals like Venice and Cannes do and how they carry films from one country to the world.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Cinema Around the World
levels.objective: After this level you can compare how Italy, France, Japan, India, Hong Kong and Nigeria each shaped cinema, and trace their influence on each other.

levels.title: From Radio to Television
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how American television borrowed its networks, shows and advertisers from radio.

levels.title: The Network Era
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how three national networks shaped what nearly all Americans watched from the 1950s to the 1970s.

levels.title: Live TV's Golden Age
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why early TV drama was performed live and what changed when shows moved to film and videotape.

levels.title: The Sitcom
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the situation comedy works and how I Love Lucy's filmed, three-camera method made reruns possible.

levels.title: TV News
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how television news grew from short bulletins into the evening news and brought events like the Vietnam War into homes.

levels.title: Ads and Ratings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how advertising paid for broadcast TV and how ratings measured audiences to set its price.

levels.title: Public and Children's TV
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why public broadcasting was created in 1967 and how shows like Sesame Street set out to teach.

levels.title: Cable Changes TV
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how cable and satellite channels ended the network era by serving smaller, targeted audiences.

levels.title: Streaming and the Binge
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how streaming changed when, where and how people watch, and how series were written for binge viewing.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Television
levels.objective: After this level you can trace television from radio's networks to streaming and explain what drove each change.

levels.title: New Hollywood
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a new generation of directors took creative control in Hollywood between the late 1960s and 1980, and what they borrowed from the New Wave.

levels.title: Jaws and the Blockbuster
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Jaws in 1975 set the summer blockbuster pattern of wide release and heavy TV advertising.

levels.title: Movies at Home
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how videotape rental changed how films earned money and why the Betamax case of 1984 mattered.

levels.title: Independent Film
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes a film independent and how low budgets can push filmmakers toward new ideas.

levels.title: Miniatures and Matte Paintings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how models, forced perspective and painted backgrounds created impossible places before computers.

levels.title: Stop Motion
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how stop-motion animators move a model a tiny step for every frame, from King Kong in 1933 onward.

levels.title: Hand-Drawn Animation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how cel animation works and why Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs in 1937 was a gamble.

levels.title: Computers Make Pictures
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how computer-generated imagery builds a scene from models, textures and light, leading to Toy Story in 1995.

levels.title: From Film to Digital
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh what filmmakers gained and lost as digital cameras and projectors replaced film stock.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Blockbusters to Pixels
levels.objective: After this level you can reason about how business and technology together changed what films got made after 1967.

levels.title: Reading a Frame
levels.objective: After this level you can analyze a single frame by looking at composition, setting, costume and where the actors stand.

levels.title: Color and Mood
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a film's color palette and grading steer mood, and spot it in a scene.

levels.title: How Editing Steers You
levels.objective: After this level you can spot how pacing, what is shown and what is held back in the edit shape what a viewer feels and believes.

levels.title: How Music Steers You
levels.objective: After this level you can spot how a score cues emotions, and test it by imagining a scene with different music or silence.

levels.title: Kinds of Documentary
levels.objective: After this level you can tell expository, observational and participatory documentaries apart and say what each one is best at.

levels.title: Is a Documentary True?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh how choices of framing, editing and reenactment can shape a documentary's truth without inventing facts.

levels.title: From Book to Screen
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a film must cut, compress or show differently when it adapts a book, and judge an adaptation on its own terms.

levels.title: Who Is the Author of a Film?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the auteur theory, which credits the director, against the view of film as a team effort.

levels.title: How to Watch Closely
levels.objective: After this level you can use a simple method to watch any film or episode closely, separating how it was made from whether you liked it.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Film & TV
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Film & TV Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
